sentence: The text is split into tokens, and each token gets its id number. The models in this app use one token per character.
Each token id picks one row of numbers from the embedding table.
Position numbers are added to each token's embedding, so the model gets a signal of the order of the text.
The embedding plus the position numbers is where the residual stream starts, before the first block.
Multi-head attention runs several attention heads side by side, each with its own query, key and value matrices.
Multi-head attention reads a normalised copy of the stream and adds its result back to the stream.
The feed-forward layer reads a normalised copy of the stream and adds its result back to the stream.
After the last block, a final norm and the output layer turn the stream into a score for every character the model knows.
Softmax turns the scores into probabilities, and sampling picks one character from them.
The new character is added to the text, and the model runs again to pick the one after it.
Learning adjusts the embedding numbers: they start random, and training changes them.
When the position numbers are learned, as in the Fables model, learning adjusts them too. The sine and cosine kind is fixed and is not adjusted.
Learning adjusts the attention weights, the matrices that make each head's queries, keys and values.
Learning adjusts the feed-forward weights.
Learning adjusts the output layer, the weights that turn the final vector into one score per character.
The family tree's first split is the idea of Rules versus learning: some programs follow behaviour a person wrote, others learn it from examples or from reward.
An expert system is the written-rules side of Rules versus learning: a person wrote every rule, and nothing in it is learned from examples.
Search and learning by reward both weigh what comes later: search looks ahead through the moves before it chooses, and learning by reward learns from rewards that may come many steps after a choice.

Learning by reward also changes numbers a little at a time, as in the Learning lesson, but it moves them towards the rewards its moves led to rather than towards examples of right answers, and here it keeps a table instead of using gradients.

A filter, like the feed-forward layer, multiplies numbers by learned weights and adds them up, and both use the same weights at every position; a filter's sum takes in only a small window of neighbouring pixels.
An image network's first layer is a set of learned filters like these; its later layers read the feature maps they make.
A memory network carries everything it has read in one vector, passed on from character to character; attention instead lets each position look back at every earlier position directly, in one step.

Both carry one vector that is changed step by step, but in different directions: a memory network's memory is carried along the text, one character to the next, while the residual stream is carried up through the blocks, separately at each position.

The two classic methods in the Classic machine learning lab also learn from examples, but without the gradients of the Learning lesson: a decision tree searches for its questions, and nearest neighbours simply keeps every example.
Rules versus learning is a first look at learning: a small table of scores that improves from examples, beside a writer that follows hand-written rules.
Training a model puts learning to work: it adjusts every number in a transformer, using the text you choose.
The architecture map shows the whole model on one page, with every part in its place.
Step through follows one prediction through the model, part by part, with the real numbers.
Scale counts the numbers in each part of the model, and compares the total with GPT-2 and GPT-3.
